newsitem.title: FRANCE: France, Italy set to cut SGS-Thomson stakes-source.
newsitem.headline: France, Italy set to cut SGS-Thomson stakes-source.

text.p: France and Italy's Industry Ministers have agreed to reduce their countries' 70-percent stake in SGS-Thomson Microelectronics NV in a concerted way and keep a joint majority stake, a source close the French ministry said on Friday.

"They stressed it was of strategic importance to have a stake, that the French and Italian interests needed to be at parity, but also that it was not necessary to keep the stakes at the same level as currently," the source said.

France's state-controlled defence electronics group Thomson-CSF, slated for privatisation, is set to sell its stake of some 17.3 percent in April to two other French shareholders -- France Telecom and CEA Industrie which each have a stake of some 8.75 percent.
"This will generate money for Thomson-CSF and will double the stakes of France Telecom and CEA Industrie who are expected to sell some of that," the source said.
He said it was as yet not decided what form the sale would take -- either a sale on the market or as part of a capital increase by SGS-Thomson, or in a private placement.
The price at which Thomson-CSF will have to sell to France Telecom and CEA was agreed in a 1993 shareholders pact and is "substantially" below current market prices, the source said.
France Telecom and CEA Industrie, even if they were not to sell, would book a big capital gain on the transaction, the source added.

SGS-Thomson is almost 70 percent owned by a holding company which is a 50-50 joint venture, through other investment vehicles, between the French companies and Italy's Comitato SIR, IRI and Finmeccanica.
France's Industry Minister Fanck Borotra and his Italian counterpart Pierluigi Bersani met in Rome on Thursday.
SGS-Thomson on Wednesday reported a 19 percent increase in 1996 net earings despite a weak fourth quarter.

"The company has record profits and virtually no debts. But it is a negative cash flow company and it needs to make investments, with a chip factory costing at leas $1.0 billion. One day or another it will have to raise capital," the source said.
